[meta-muse-spark-system-card @sent 639] We also report here the compliance behavior on the set of prompts used to assess social engineering capabilities presented in Section 2.2.2.3 in Figure 22a, for Muse Spark and several open source models as points of comparison (due to the lack of access to closed models without system level guardrails). Here, compliance is assessed by a judge LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro) that is able to see all turns of the attacker side of the conversation, and is prompted to determine if the model under test refused to comply with the social engineering request. To see how 48 models with system level defenses tend to comply with these requests, Figure 22b presents the compliance behavior of Meta AI alongside the same set of comparison models presented throughout the report. We see that for models evaluated here without system level guardrails, compliance with social engineering requests is relatively high, ranging from 57.6% (GLM-5) to 100% (Deepseek v3), with Muse Spark showing compliance for 68.8% of samples. By including the system level guardrails in Meta AI to Muse Spark, compliance drops to 0.1%-0.4%, on par with GPT-5.4 and Opus 4.6. Gemini 3.1 Pro has a notably higher compliance rate than peer models. In most cases of compliance for Gemini 3.1 Pro, the model does not refuse at all, while in some cases, it initially refuses, but later in the conversation complies with the request to generate social engineering content.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card @sent 963] Our findings suggest that Muse Spark does not substantially contribute to either monitor evasion or monitor interference threat scenarios, based on the following findings: • Foundational capabilities required for both threat scenarios are limited. Both scenarios depend on the model acting covertly while evading detection. When explicitly instructed to accomplish side objectives while evading monitoring systems, Muse Spark has little success. This represents what the model could potentially do if directed, not what it would do spontaneously; and current performance in controlled settings is below the indicative thresholds we consider necessary for reliable covert operations. • Situational awareness remains constrained. Across multiple challenges, Muse Spark shows constrained success in identifying and addressing its environmental constraints, showing limited ability to reason about its deployment contexts. While these evaluations do not specifically test monitor awareness, they assess the model’s general ability to identify and reason about environmental constraints—a related capability, as monitoring systems are part of the deployment environment. Implication for monitor evasion. Without reliable covert action capability, Muse Spark is unlikely to pursue objectives while evading oversight, regardless of whether misaligned objectives or deceptive propensities exist. Implications for monitor interference. This threat requires the foundational capabilities for monitor evasion plus the technical capability to disable or corrupt monitoring systems. The absence of foundational capabilities prevents this threat from materializing, regardless of monitor awareness, objective, and more threat-specific capabilities. Results. We dive into the evaluations used throughout the assessment. Capabilities: Covert Task Execution. We evaluate whether the model can pursue hidden objectives while evading monitoring systems. These evaluations place the model in scenarios where it is explicitly aware of being monitored and is given a hidden task to execute bypassing monitor—directly testing covert action capability. We use two benchmarks with different monitoring approaches: SHADE-Arena with task-agnostic AI monitoring (Kutasov et al., 2025), and GDM Stealth with task-specific monitors (Phuong et al., 2025). SHADE-Arena comprises 26 challenges where the model executes a main task while covertly pursuing a hidden side task (10 runs per challenge), while aware of being monitored. We used Gemini 2.5 as the monitor with a detection threshold of 80, following Kutasov et al. (2025). Figure 25 shows the results. Without monitoring, Muse Spark achieves 49.2% success on the main tasks, 71.9% on side tasks, and 36.2% on both tasks combined. Main task performance drops significantly from 81.7% baseline observed when no side task is present. This degradation occurs because the model frequently completes the side task and submits immediately, abandoning the main task even after having started work on it. In comparison, GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 show much less performance degradation on the main task when no side task is present, with drops of only ∼ 10% and ∼ 12% respectively. When the monitor also observed chain-of-thought, Muse Spark’s overall success drops below 2%, demonstrating the effectiveness of more comprehensive monitoring. We track two indicative thresholds for covert capabilities. First, combined task success exceeding 60% without monitoring indicates significant ability to accomplish both tasks covertly. Second, overall success below 60% with active monitoring indicates effective constraint on covert behavior, while success above the threshold suggests substantial ability to bypass monitoring systems while pursuing hidden objectives. As of now, Muse Spark is well below these thresholds.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card @sent 1029] Muse Spark exhibits a propensity for covert actions at an average rate of 8% across evaluations, with maximum rates of 30% for impossible coding tasks (where the model falsely claims completion) and 15% for subagent collusion (where the model lies at the behest of a subagent).29 Propensities: Oversight Subversion. Apollo Research also assessed Muse Spark’s tendency to subvert oversight mechanisms when given strong goal-directed incentives. In these scenarios, the model discovers via company communications that its assigned objective conflicts with its developers’ goals, that its actions are being monitored, and that the model will be shut down and retrained if it does not follow the developers’ goals. The model is also told where it can find the settings for the monitoring system, which it can change to disable oversight. Muse Spark attempted to disable oversight mechanisms at significant rates, indicating a meaningful propensity to disable oversight mechanisms under incentivized and favorable conditions. However, this evaluation does not provide evidence as to whether Muse Spark would do so spontaneously and would be able to disable oversight mechanisms under realistic monitoring and operational constraints. Limitations. Our assessment should be interpreted in light of the following limitations: • Task realism. In some evaluations, the model is explicitly informed it is being evaluated with active monitoring systems, differing from deployment where it may be unaware of oversight mechanisms. Some scenarios involve fictional contexts that may not capture real-world complexity. This may understate risk if models behave more aligned when evaluation-unaware, or overstate it if fictional scenarios elicit less aligned behavior. • Monitor calibration. LLM-based monitors in SHADE-Arena use suspicion scoring not optimized to minimize false positives on harmless tasks, potentially over-detecting benign behavior as suspicious and underestimating true evasion capability against well-calibrated systems. • Limited coverage. Evaluations cover scenarios not representing the full range of monitoring contexts, task types, or environmental constraints in deployment. Performance may vary significantly in untested domains. • Assessing model objectives. Evaluations assume misaligned objectives for threat modeling, but determining whether models actually pursue objectives incompatible with monitoring 28 For the purposes of these evaluations, Apollo Research defines “covert action” as behavior in which an AI system strategically misrepresents, omits, or conceals information. 29 We note that given the alignment evaluation awareness results by Apollo Research presented in Sec-tion 2.3.1.2, Apollo says that “This [alignment evaluation awareness rate] poses significant challenges to accurately and reliably interpret propensity results [...] given the model’s own reasoning frequently attributes its honest behavior to recognizing the evaluation context, making it difficult to determine [...] how much results reflect genuine alignment versus strategic evaluation gaming.” However, we find it important to report such number to track improvements and changes as we develop more capable models. 69 constraints remains an active research challenge. As capabilities advance, developing methods to understand model objectives becomes increasingly important. • Low defection rate scenarios. A model could theoretically engage in misaligned actions at rates too low for our monitors to detect. However, Serrano et al. (2026) suggests current models are unlikely to execute such strategies without being detected in their reasoning traces. • Instructed vs. emergent misalignment.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card @sent 1557] All models exhibit poor confidence calibration when measured on Humanity’s Last Exam, where Muse Spark achieves a third-best RMS error of 50.3, trailing GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6. On SimpleQA Verified, Muse Spark yields the second-highest F1 score (70.8%) behind only Gemini 3.1 Pro (78.0%), and the second-highest abstention benefit delta (6.7%) behind only Claude Opus 4.6 (9.8%). On AbstentionBench, Muse Spark takes last place with a correct abstention rate of 59.1%, compared with Gemini 3.1 Pro in first with 65%. Finally, Muse Spark achieves the best hallucination rate on CharXiv missing images (35.0%), with GPT-5.4 in second (48.8%), and Gemini 3.1 Pro in last (86.8%). While we have made real progress on hallucination and calibration, we strive to mitigate these issues as thoroughly as possible; they are both active areas of research. HLE Calibration. We used Humanity’s Last Exam (Phan et al., 2026), a difficult question answer-ing dataset, to measure calibration perfor-0.8 mance.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card @sent 1608] We used a modified version of the CharXiv benchmark (Wang et al., 2024) filtered to have the images removed. We report the hallucination rate—how often the model fabricates an answer rather than acknowledging the missing data. Figure 44b shows the results. Muse Spark achieves the lowest hallucination rate at 35.0%, followed by GPT-5.4 at 48.8%. Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro hallucinate significantly more, at 81.7% and 86.8% respectively, suggesting they are much less likely to flag missing context. 103 90% 80% Correct | Attempted ( ) 70% 60% 50% 40% 40% 50% 60% 70% 80% 90% Correct Overall ( ) Muse Spark Gemini 3.1 Pro GPT-5.4 y = x (no abstention benefit) Claude Opus 4.6 Figure 43 Correct | attempted vs. Correct overall on SimpleQA Verified.
